title: Yom Kippur: ask first
hook: before the day, people ask one another's forgiveness

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shabbat Shuvah and Hosea's call. Your line was return. Which dropped good thing did you go back to? Today, the one thing Yom Kippur can't do by itself. Day six hundred fifty-two.

The afternoon before Yom Kippur has its own sounds. Phones buzzing with messages: if I hurt you this year, I'm sorry. Neighbors stopping each other on the street. A teenager, mortified, knocking on a sister's bedroom door. Some of it is a little formal, a habit. Some of it is the hardest conversation of the year. People do this because of one line in the Mishnah, and once you hear it, the whole holiday looks different.
screen: `PHONES BUZZING: I'M SORRY.` → `A KNOCK ON A SISTER'S DOOR.` → `ONE LINE IN THE MISHNAH.`

segments.voice: The line is at the very end of tractate Yoma, the Mishnah's book about Yom Kippur. Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah teaches: for wrongs between a person and God, Yom Kippur atones. For wrongs between a person and another person, Yom Kippur does not atone, until you have appeased the other person. Read that again. The holiest day of the year, a whole day of fasting and prayer, the high point of the calendar, cannot fix what you did to your neighbor. Only your neighbor can. So you go first. You ask. The Talmud and later law work out the details with real psychological sense. You should be specific, not vague. If the person refuses, you try again, up to three times, and bring a few friends along to help make peace. If they still refuse after that, the burden lifts from you. And there's a rule for the other side, too. Maimonides writes that a person shouldn't be cruel and refuse to forgive. When someone sincerely asks, forgive with a whole heart and a willing spirit. Not every hurt can be fixed in an afternoon. Teachers are careful to say that forgiveness isn't the same as trust, and that no one is required to put themselves back in danger. But the shape is clear. Before you stand before God asking to be forgiven, stand in front of the people you hurt. Then the day can do its work. The word for this kind of forgiveness, mechilah, has the sense of letting go of a debt.
screen: `BETWEEN YOU AND GOD.` · `BETWEEN YOU AND YOUR NEIGHBOR.` · `UP TO THREE TIMES.` · `DON'T BE CRUEL; FORGIVE.` · then, large: `ASK BEFORE THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask forgiveness from someone. Bring to mind one person you hurt, even a little: a sharp word, a broken promise, a silence. Picture their face. Find the specific thing. Now say, quietly, the words you'd use: I'm sorry for, and the thing itself. Then decide how you'll reach them, today or soon. If you pray, you can ask God for the courage to make the call. Then, for a moment, think of someone who might be waiting to ask you. The bell holds the time.
Yom Kippur. The day of atonement, which, the Mishnah says, can't atone for wrongs between people until they make peace.
Your line: ask before the day. Today, make the call or send the message: I'm sorry for, and the specific thing. Day six hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: In the days before Yom Kippur, especially on its eve, many Jews ask family, friends and coworkers for forgiveness (mechilah), and many say a prayer before Kol Nidre declaring that they forgive anyone who wronged them.

original.note: Hebrew: forgiveness, pardon, with the sense of forgoing a debt.

trapdoor: what you thought: Yom Kippur wipes the slate clean.
what it means: only the person you hurt can forgive what you did to them; you ask first.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Yoma 8:9, Yoma 87a on asking three times, and Maimonides, Hilchot Teshuvah 2:9–10.

notes: Mishnah Yoma 8:9 teaching attributed to Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah; confirm.
Asking up to three times, with three people each time: Yoma 87a as codified (Shulchan Arukh OC 606:1); confirm.
Maimonides Hilchot Teshuvah 2:10: do not be cruel; forgive with a whole heart; confirm.
Forgiveness vs. trust and safety: a widely taught modern clarification, not from these sources; a Keeper may want a citation.
mechilah as 'forgoing a debt' is a common explanation; confirm.
